blocks.text: It is impossible to determine the lattice energy of a compound by a single direct experiment. We can, however, calculate the value for ΔH°latt using several experimental data and an energy cycle called the Born–Haber cycle. Born-Haber cycle is an application of Hess’ law. Let us consider calculation of lattice energy of sodium Chloride using hess’s law and Born-Haber cycle.

blocks.alt: Triangle of three light-blue boxes: Na(s) + 1/2 Cl2(g) (top left), Na+Cl-(s) (top right) and Na+(g) + Cl-(g) (bottom). Arrow top left to top right: delta H(o)f. Arrow from the elements down to the gaseous ions: delta Hx. Arrow from the gaseous ions up to Na+Cl-(s): delta H(o)latt.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.8: Enthalpy cycle of sodium chloride (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.8).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 6.8 gives the product as Na⁺Cl⁻(g) and draws the lattice-energy arrow from the solid to the gaseous ions. The product is solid NaCl, Na⁺Cl⁻(s), and the lattice energy is released from the gaseous ions to the solid, as drawn above.

items: ΔH°f : standard enthalpy of formation of NaCl can be measured conveniently in a calorimeter.

blocks.text: The above energy triangle has been extended to show the various stages involved in finding ΔHx. The complete energy cycle is called the Born-Haber cycle and it is presented in Figure 6.9.

blocks.alt: Born-Haber ladder, not to scale. From the reactants level Na(s) + 1/2 Cl2(g): up by delta Hat of Na = +108 kJ mol-1 to Na(g) + 1/2 Cl2(g); up by delta Hi of Na = +496 kJ mol-1 to Na+(g) + e- + 1/2 Cl2(g); up by delta Hat of Cl2 = +121 kJ mol-1 to Na+(g) + e- + Cl(g); down by delta Hea of Cl = -349 kJ mol-1 to Na+(g) + Cl-(g); a thick arrow down, delta Hlatt = ? (lattice energy of NaCl), to the final product Na+Cl-(s). From the reactants an arrow goes down to Na+Cl-(s): delta Hf = -411.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 6.9 writes ‘Na⁺(g) + ½ Cl₂’ where Na(g) + ½ Cl₂(g) is meant, and ‘Cl₂(g)’ at the top where Cl(g) is meant; both are drawn correctly above.
